author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: A Game Neither of Us Wins
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
I won the first game of Pai Sho because Iroh wasn't paying attention.

That should have been impossible.

He'd taught me the opening himself, explaining the balance between movement and patience with the kind of delight most people reserved for a very good dessert. I was improving, but only in the way a determined student improves when the teacher is much better and very kind.

Yet here he was, staring at a tile instead of the board.

"I think that's the end," I said.

He looked up.

"Is it?"

I pointed.

He studied the position for several seconds, then set down the tile in his hand.

"So it is."

I sat back.

"You've never surrendered that quickly."

"I am capable of losing."

"Yes, but you usually lose while delivering a lecture about why losing is good for the soul."

He smiled, though it didn't quite reach his eyes.

The teahouse was quiet. A light rain tapped the repaired roof. The new affordable house blend had sold well enough to cover the week's deliveries, and a small packet of mountain mint sat on the shelf, carefully saved for special occasions. There was no emergency that required either of us to stay awake.

Which left the problem Iroh wasn't saying aloud.

"Are you worried about something?" I asked.

He folded his hands.

"Only the ordinary things."

"That is not an answer."

"Then perhaps you have learned another lesson."

I waited.

He looked at the board.

"Earlier, a visitor asked whether you and Maui would be attending the next Lantern Walk together."

"Possibly."

"They seemed pleased by the thought."

"People like watching him make a fool of himself with decorations."

"Yes. He is very enthusiastic."

Iroh smiled, then let it fade.

"I found myself wondering whether there would still be room for tea that evening."

There it was.

I didn't laugh. The vulnerability in his voice didn't deserve a joke, even though I wanted to soften it.

"Would you like to make plans with me?" I asked.

He looked at me.

"I would. But I did not wish to sound as though I were asking you to choose."

"You can ask for time without asking me to stop caring about other people."

He nodded slowly.

"We have discussed ethical non-monogamy and polyamory before," he said. "I understand that love need not be a contest. Still, I find that understanding does not prevent a foolish thought from visiting."

"You're not foolish."

"I am sometimes."

"All right. You can be foolish. But you don't have to hide it."

He looked at me, and some of the tension eased.

I moved the Pai Sho board aside.

"Tell me what you're afraid of."

He took a breath.

"That I will become the pleasant place you visit when you need rest, and then leave behind when you are ready for excitement."

I felt the words settle between us.

"I love this place," I said. "But I don't love you because you're restful. I love you because you tell me when I'm being impatient. Because you remember the names of people the square forgets. Because you have a terrible sense of humor and an even worse habit of making me tea when I haven't asked."

He chuckled.

"And because you're willing to tell me when you're frightened," I added. "Even when it's difficult."

"I have not been particularly brave tonight."

"You have."

We sat in silence for a while. The rain moved across the roof in uneven rhythms. Somewhere beyond the kitchen, the repaired gutter clicked as water passed through it.

"Would it help to plan our next evening?" I asked.

"Yes."

"Then let's look at the calendar."

We did.

I had promised to help Greg with the listening fair at Starwake. Maui wanted assistance checking the sea-glass orchard after a storm. Katara was still away in the South, and I had agreed to help organize supplies for the Riverstone clinic volunteers. None of those commitments were romantic emergencies. They were part of the life I had chosen.

The calendar had a mark beside the Listening Fair that Iroh didn't recognize.

"A small circle," he said. "Does that mean you have promised to perform?"

"No. It means Greg invited me to help. I haven't agreed to a shift."

He looked relieved. "Then you can still decide."

"Yes. And so can he."

We took out a separate page for the promises I'd actually made. The difference between an invitation and a commitment had been a hard lesson for everyone in the vale. It was particularly hard for Iroh, who'd spent years interpreting a request for help as something he should fulfill before anybody could ask twice.

"Can I be selfish for a moment?" he asked.

"Please."

"I would like one evening where you come to the shop without having to explain what comes next. I know you may visit other people. I only want to enjoy this moment without planning the next parting."

The wish surprised me. Iroh so often answered with warm patience that I'd begun to forget he could be afraid of running out of time.

"I can do that tonight," I said. "Tomorrow I have plans I intend to keep."

"Then tonight."

His shoulders eased. He touched the Pai Sho tile we'd left at the edge of the board.

"Would you like a rematch?"

"Not if you're going to let me win."

"An outrageous suggestion. I intend to defeat you magnificently."

I laughed and moved my first piece. For a while we played badly on purpose, making up ridiculous commentary for each tile. The outside world still held people I loved and work I wanted to do. Here was a man who wanted to tease me over a board game, not ask me to prove that he was the most important road in my life.

When the kettle began to hiss, he looked up at me with an expression so fond I forgot my strategy. He took the opportunity to win a piece.

"Cheater," I accused.

"An old general must take the opportunities available."

I was still laughing when we put the board away.

We found an evening for tea, then another for a walk through Jasmine Steps.

Iroh looked at the page.

"That is a rather large number of people in your life."

"Yes."

He smiled.

"And yet you are here."

"I am."

He reached across the table for my hand.

"Then perhaps I should stop making a question of what is already an answer."

"Not stop asking questions," I said. "Just ask me the real ones."

He nodded.

I picked up the Pai Sho tile I'd won with.

"One more game?"

He looked at the board.

"You are taking advantage of an elderly man in emotional distress."

"Absolutely."

"Shameless."

"Very."

He reset the tiles.

This time he paid attention.

I lost in twelve moves.

"That's more like it," I said.

"I hope the defeat was instructive."

"Deeply."

He laughed.

After the game, we carried the cups into the small second kitchen. The roof no longer leaked, but the room still felt intimate in a way the public teahouse did not. He stood close enough that I could smell the citrus in his sleeve.

"May I offer you something other than tea?" he asked.

"That depends."

"On what?"

"Whether the offer involves another strategic defeat."

He leaned closer.

"I had hoped for a kiss."

I smiled.

"That seems fair."

His hand rested at my waist, warm and steady. I kissed him slowly, then again when he murmured something about me having very poor negotiating skills. The kettle began to hiss. We ignored it for just long enough to make the joke inevitable.

"Even the kettle has opinions," I whispered.

"It always has."

We spent the rest of the evening together after closing, private and unhurried. The next morning we still had to count the tea stock and write to the growers. The world had not rearranged itself to remove every fear.

But when Iroh set out the Pai Sho board again, he met my eyes.

"Perhaps," he said, "I will let you win one day."

"That sounds suspiciously like cheating."

"Then I shall have to win honestly."

He did.
